364256.title: Exceptional-parameter conjecture for biased edge coloring games
364256.review_depth: Current v2 (Discrete Appl. Math. 2025) read: definitions (Maker colours m edges per turn, Breaker one; Breaker wins if the mover cannot colour), Proposition 1.1, Theorems 4.2-4.3 (wheels; W4 gives the printed pair (3,2)), Proposition 5.1 (exceptional pairs, proof omitted), Conjecture 5.2.
364256.mathematical_attempts: Mechanism analysis only: the conjecture needs a witness graph for EVERY non-exceptional pair (m1,m2), i.e. whenever (m2+1) does not divide (m1+1). A tempo/zugzwang design (trap component plus isolated-edge padding, entry forced by move index mod m+1) is the natural route, but Maker may enter the trap with several consecutive moves, so a uniform strategy proof for all pairs would be needed; one pair from a small exhaustive game search would be a zero-credit partial instance. No citing work found (web search 2026-11-05). Lean cost of uniform game-strategy proofs is very high.
364256.remaining_gap: A uniform family G(m1,m2) with a full two-sided strategy analysis for every non-exceptional pair.

364481.title: Injectivity of pairwise products of partition parts
364481.review_depth: Source v1 Conjectures 1-3, Proposition 1 (length <= 3) and Proposition 2 (binary partitions) read in full.
364481.mathematical_attempts: This lane independently found a short full proof: with phi(t) = sum of lambda_i^t, equal pre_2 gives phi_l(2t) - phi_m(2t) = (phi_l(t) - phi_m(t)) (phi_l(t) + phi_m(t)); equal size makes the difference vanish at t = 1, hence at every 2^j, and a dominant-term argument forces lambda = mu. Also: no length-4 pairwise-product collision with equal sums exists (the reciprocal involution then fixes the multiset; search to part 60 in logs/pre2_len4-60.log). BUT the conjecture is already proved: Stella Li, "A note on multiset reconstruction from sum and pairwise products", arXiv:2508.00971 (abstract and HTML retained), and a 2026 Integers note; a further 2026 paper (Garg, arXiv:2606.09321) cites the result. Zero credit.

364715.title: Conjecture on the complexity of the k-general d-position problem
364715.review_depth: Source Section 7 problem statement read: input (G, k >= 2, d >= 1, r).
364715.mathematical_attempts: k and d are part of the input; restricted to k = 3 the problem is the general d-position problem, NP-complete by Klavzar-Rall-Yero (arXiv:2005.08095, Theorem 2.2). Membership in NP: for a candidate set S, the maximum number of S-vertices on a u-v geodesic of length <= d is computable by a DP over the shortest-path DAG for every pair, so verification is polynomial. A full proof is a routine bridge. Zero credit.
364715.remaining_gap: None for credit (routine). A fixed-k hardness classification would be a different question.

364839.title: Characterization of Castelnuovo triplets
364839.review_depth: Full source read (Hamano-Sainose-Hibi, Australas. J. Combin. 90 (2024)): definition (Castelnuovo = equality in Hibi volume bound), Theorems 1.6 and 3.2, Corollary 2.2, Conjecture 3.3, Examples 3.4-3.5; Tsuchiya arXiv:2010.13617 Theorems 1.3-1.5 (h*-characterisation) read.
364839.mathematical_attempts: Equivalent h* form: Castelnuovo iff h* = (1,h,...,h,c), h = b + c - d - 1; conjecture is h <= (c+1)(d+1) for c >= 2. Hand computation: prisms R x [0,c+1] over a one-interior-point polygon are Castelnuovo only for the 3-boundary-point triangle (exactly the printed Q(c), attaining the bound). Exact random scouting in d = 3 with a checker validated on all printed examples (cube, Example 3.5, Q(c), P_{c,d}(n)): 4000 + 150000 samples of 6-7 points in [-2,2]^3, 60000 samples of 8 points in [-3,3]^3. Castelnuovo polytopes with c = 1 reached b = 34 (> 29 printed), but c >= 2 examples had b <= 11; no violation. Any counterexample would need a Lean proof of a Lebesgue volume and lattice-point counts: high Lean cost.
364839.remaining_gap: A structural proof of the upper bound (e.g. via collinearity of interior points for c >= 2) or a c >= 2 polytope with b > cd + 2d + 2.

365134.title: The Hamiltonian-path conjecture for non-conflicting flows
365134.review_depth: Full read of definitions (Definition 3, Remark 3), Lemma 1, Theorem 4 (2-factor with <= 2 cycles), Proposition 5 (P10), Theorem 5 (infinite 2-edge-connected family), Conjectures 7-8, Problems 1-2 of arXiv:2410.04389 (Australas. J. Combin. 91(3) 2025); r89 sibling 365133 noted.
365134.mathematical_attempts: Exact reformulation: a non-conflicting flow w.r.t. perfect matching F is a labelling of F-edges by a, b, g = a+b with every Fbar-cycle summing to 0 (#a+#g and #b+#g even per cycle) and no Fbar edge joining a and b; 3-edge-colourable graphs are trivial. Checker validated: P10 has no flow; source Theorem 5 graph (l = 1, 34 vertices, all 96 perfect matchings) has no flow; witnesses for 5 named snarks re-verified independently. Coverage: (i) all labelled cubic multigraphs on Hamilton path 0..n-1 for n = 10, 12, 14 (2205, 29295, 446985 completions; only failures are the two labelled Petersen copies at n = 10); simple n = 16 only 1/32 chunk (81722 completions, 249 non-colourable, all with flow). Probe shows every bridgeless Ham-path cubic (multi)graph with n <= 12 (multi) and n = 14 (simple) has a 2-factor with <= 2 cycles, so this range is already covered by the source Theorem 4. (ii) Beyond Theorem 4: the P10-e block analysis (block with both cut edges in F always conflicts; otherwise it acts as a "twisted" Fbar edge forbidding equal non-g labels) shows a Ham-path graph contains at most two Petersen blocks (P10-e or P10-v, neither traversable). All bridgeless base multigraphs with Hamilton path on m <= 10 vertices with two end edges replaced by P10-e (8008 graphs), both ends replaced by P10-v (2300) and mixed (4204): every one admits a flow; each of these has all 2-factors with >= 3 cycles. Also P10 with any triangle/digon insertions (308 graphs), Blanusa-type dot products, 2-sums, J5, J7: all have flows. No counterexample.
365134.remaining_gap: A proof for graphs whose 2-factors all have >= 3 cycles, or a counterexample needing a forcing mechanism with at most two rigid Petersen blocks.
